reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Presents with persistent or recurrent perianal discharge, irritation, and intermittent swelling or abscess, often following drainage of a previous anorectal abscess
A fistula is an abnormal epithelialised track connecting the anal canal or rectum (internal opening) to the perianal skin (external opening)
Goodsall's rule helps predict the internal opening: anterior external openings tend to track radially, while posterior ones tend to curve to the posterior midline
Fistulae are classified by their relationship to the sphincter complex (intersphincteric, transsphincteric, suprasphincteric, extrasphincteric) which determines treatment and continence risk
The primary treatment goal is to eradicate sepsis and close the track while preserving continence
Low, simple fistulae may be laid open (fistulotomy), whereas high or complex tracks require sphincter-sparing options such as seton drainage, advancement flaps, or LIFT procedures
Multiple, complex, or recurrent fistulae, especially with proctitis, should raise suspicion of Crohn's disease, tuberculosis, or malignancy
A draining (loose) seton controls sepsis and maintains drainage while definitive management is planned
reference.pathophysiology: Most anal fistulae are the chronic sequel of a cryptoglandular anorectal abscess. After the abscess drains, the primary infected anal gland at the dentate line persists and an epithelialised or granulation-lined track remains between the internal opening in the anal canal and the external opening on the skin. Ongoing low-grade infection prevents healing. The track's course through the sphincter complex determines its classification and the surgical risk to continence. Secondary causes include Crohn's disease, tuberculosis, radiation, trauma, and malignancy, which produce more complex and refractory fistulae.
additionalInvestigations: Examination under anaesthesia to define internal and external openings and the track
MRI pelvis for complex, recurrent, or suspected Crohn's-related fistulae
Endoanal ultrasound, sometimes with hydrogen peroxide enhancement, to map the track
Endoscopy and biopsy when inflammatory bowel disease or malignancy is suspected
redFlags: Complex, branching, or recurrent fistulae suggesting Crohn's disease or malignancy
Associated undrained sepsis with systemic upset requiring urgent drainage
Rapidly progressive perianal sepsis suggesting necrotising infection
Induration or a mass raising concern for underlying carcinoma
reference.prognosis: Simple low fistulae have high cure rates after fistulotomy with minimal continence impact. Complex, high, or Crohn's-related fistulae are prone to recurrence and require staged sphincter-preserving strategies, with a persistent risk of continence disturbance.
pitfalls: Laying open a high transsphincteric or suprasphincteric fistula and causing incontinence
Failing to identify and address the internal opening, leading to recurrence
Overlooking Crohn's disease in complex or recurrent disease
Creating a false track by forceful probing
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Surgical eradication of the track while preserving continence, with fistulotomy (laying open) for low, simple fistulae
Sphincter-sparing techniques for high or complex tracks, including seton drainage, ligation of the intersphincteric fistula tract and mucosal advancement flaps
Drainage of any associated anorectal abscess and control of active sepsis, often with a loose seton, before definitive repair
For Crohn's-related fistulae, combined medical therapy with anti-TNF agents such as infliximab alongside seton drainage
Examination under anaesthesia and MRI or endoanal ultrasound to map the track relative to the sphincter complex
Colorectal surgical referral, with biopsy where inflammatory bowel disease or malignancy is suspected
